2310538.title: Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation Organises 12th District Collectors’ Peyjal Samvad
2310538.body_html:
Ministry of Jal Shakti
Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation Organises 12th District Collectors’ Peyjal Samvad
Six Districts Showcase Innovative Practices on Source Sustainability, Behaviour Change through IEC activities, Grievance Redressal Mechanism and Convergence
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 5:36PM by PIB Delhi

The Department of Drinking Water & Sanitation (DDWS), Ministry of Jal Shakti, organised the 12th edition of the District Collectors’ Peyjal Samvad today through video conferencing, bringing together senior officials, District Collectors/ District Magistrates/ Deputy Commissioners, to deliberate on accelerating the implementation of Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0 and sharing of best practices.

The Samvad was chaired by Shri Ashok K.K. Meena, Secretary, DDWS. Shri Kamal Kishore Soan, Additional Secretary & Mission Director, National Jal Jeevan Mission (NJJM) and Senior Officers from SWSM and DDWS were also present during the Samvad.

Addressing the occasion, Shri Ashok K.K. Meena, Secretary, DDWS, emphasized the importance of regular monthly District Water and Sanitation Mission (DWSM) meetings to review scheme progress, service delivery, water quality, and source sustainability under JJM 2.0. He stressed that completed schemes should be handed over to Gram Panchayats through the Jal Arpan programme after the prescribed trial run and proper documentation, thereby promoting community ownership and sustainable operation and maintenance. He urged districts to actively involve MPs, MLAs, and other public representatives through Jal Arpan ceremonies, DISHA meetings, and DWSM reviews to enhance transparency and public confidence in rural water supply systems. He also highlighted the need for timely utilization of JJM 2.0 funds, accurate reporting of physical and financial progress, and preparation of District and State Improvement Plans to address service gaps. Further, he encouraged the use of the Decision Support System (DSS) for planning source sustainability measures such as rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge, while underscoring that regular monitoring of scheme functionality, water quality, and sustainability interventions is essential to ensure reliable and sustainable drinking water services for all rural households.

The progress and best practices of six selected districts, Shahdol (Madhya Pradesh), Samba (Jammu & Kashmir), Hooghly (West Bengal), Dhamtari (Chhattisgarh), Fatehgarh Sahib (Punjab) and North & Middle Andaman (Andaman & Nicobar Islands) were also presented by the respective District Collectors/District Magistrates/District Commissioners to facilitate cross-learning and support other districts in strengthening implementation under JJM 2.0.
Innovative Best Practices shared by six districts through presentations by the respective District Collector/ District Magistrate/ Deputy Commissioner:

  • Shahdol, Madhya Pradesh- Sh. Parth Jaiswal, District Collector informed that civil and electrical works for the water supply schemes have largely been completed, and the remaining works are expected to be commissioned by November 2026. Emphasis was laid on conducting weekly reviews to ensure timely completion of all Single Village Schemes (SVSs) and Multi Village Schemes (MVSs). Out of 544 completed SVSs, 405 have already been handed over, while 35 more are planned for handover on 2 October 2026 through the Jal Arpan programme. The district has set a target to achieve full completion and functionality of all rural water supply schemes by December 2026 and to declare the district fully functional by 26 January 2027. The district also showcased best practices, including a digital platform for overhead tank cleaning and maintenance, an online mechanism for collection of water and sanitation charges through UPI and net banking, and systems to strengthen Gram Panchayat-led operation and maintenance. These initiatives are helping improve transparency, service delivery, revenue collection, and long-term sustainability of rural drinking water infrastructure.

  • Samba, Jammu & Kashmir- Smt Ayushi Sudan, Deputy Commissioner presented Samba as a model district under Jal Jeevan Mission, despite facing significant water management challenges due to diverse geographical conditions and dependence on groundwater sources. Through JJM, the district increased Functional Household Tap Connection (FHTC) coverage with prescribed service levels from about 23% to nearly 70%, adding around 35,000 new tap connections. The district implemented 130 water supply schemes, supported by filtration plants, tube wells, dug wells, pumping stations, and storage infrastructure. Key challenges included difficult hilly terrain, declining groundwater levels, source sustainability concerns, power supply constraints, land-related issues, and the high operation and maintenance requirements of water supply systems. To address these challenges, the district adopted location-specific solutions based on local hydrogeological conditions. Several successful interventions were highlighted, including the revival of a 60-year-old dug well at the revered Uttar Behni Temple, which now provides drinking water to hundreds of households, and the development of customized schemes for remote hilly villages through a combination of filtration plants and tube wells to ensure universal coverage.

  • Hooghly, West Bengal- Sh. Khursheed Ali Qadri, District Magistrate showcased the district’s substantial progress in creating drinking water infrastructure, the district shifted its focus towards community participation, service assessment, and grievance redressal to ensure sustainable service delivery under Jal Jeevan Mission. Under the Jal Seva Abhiyan, village-level service assessments were conducted by Village Water and Sanitation Committees (VWSCs), followed by validation exercises. The findings and suggested improvements were incorporated into the District Improvement Plan and submitted to the State Government. A strong emphasis was also placed on community awareness through Self-Help Groups (SHGs), with meetings, workshops, and campaigns involving nearly seven lakh women. These initiatives focused on water conservation, efficient water use, source sustainability, and reducing water wastage. To strengthen accountability, the district established a robust grievance redressal mechanism, receiving complaints through multiple channels, including helplines, emails, public representatives, and government platforms. Dedicated public hearing days are organized every week to address drinking water-related grievances promptly. Strict action has also been taken against illegal water connections and unauthorized usage to prevent water losses and ensure equitable distribution. Regular District Water and Sanitation Committee (DWSC) and DISHA meetings are being conducted with active participation of public representatives to review JJM implementation, address concerns, and undertake corrective measures. These efforts have significantly improved community engagement, transparency, service delivery, and public confidence in rural drinking water systems.

​​​​​​​

  • Dhamtari, Chhattisgarh- Sh. Abhinash Mishra, District Collector showcased that the district reported significant progress in the implementation of MVSs, with the majority of schemes already completed and the remaining works expected to be completed after obtaining necessary clearances, particularly in forest and tiger reserve areas. To ensure effective operation and maintenance (O&M), regular DWSM meetings are being conducted twice a month, focusing on scheme sustainability, convergence activities, payment issues, and service delivery improvements. The district has strengthened community ownership by ensuring active participation of VWSCs, with user charges being collected online based on population served. Gram Panchayats have been entrusted with the day-to-day O&M of water supply assets. Special emphasis has been placed on awareness generation through SHGs and community mobilization, with women playing a leading role in water governance. More than two-thirds of the Sarpanches and community representatives involved in these initiatives are women. A notable success story highlighted was a solar-powered Single Village Scheme in a remote tribal habitation, which has significantly improved access to drinking water in difficult terrain. The initiative received wide public appreciation and demonstrated how community participation, renewable energy, and decentralized management can contribute to sustainable rural drinking water service delivery.

​​​​​​​

  • Fatehgarh Sahib, Punjab- Dr. Sona Thind, Deputy Commissioner highlighted the district’s successful achievement of 100%  FHTC coverage, ensuring tap water supply to all 78,475 rural households across 429 villages, along with full coverage of schools and Anganwadi centres. Building upon this achievement, the district has shifted its focus towards maintaining service quality, with nearly 80% of rural households receiving more than 70 lpcd of water, exceeding the JJM benchmark of 55 lpcd. To address groundwater depletion and water quality concerns, the district implemented a major 12 MLD surface water project drawing water from the Rajpura Distributary. The project serves 92 villages and has significantly benefited fluoride-affected areas by providing safe drinking water to over 86,000 people through an extensive pipeline network. The district has also adopted IoT-based real-time monitoring systems and a dedicated grievance redressal mechanism to ensure continuous service delivery and prompt response to complaints. Regular DWSM meetings, community participation through Gram Panchayats and VWSCs, and structured planning have strengthened local ownership of water supply systems. A strong emphasis has been placed on water quality surveillance, with NABL-accredited laboratories conducting regular testing and women-led community monitoring through Field Testing Kits (FTKs). Through a combination of surface water infrastructure, digital monitoring, community participation, and rigorous quality testing, the district has developed a sustainable model for maintaining safe and reliable drinking water services under Jal Jeevan Mission.

  • North and Middle Andaman, Andaman & Nicobar Islands- Sh. Sushant Padha, Deputy Commissioner highlighted the district's achievement of 100% FHTC coverage, covering all villages and approximately 24,400 households under Jal Jeevan Mission. A total of eight JJM schemes were completed with an expenditure of about ₹5.2 crore, ensuring universal rural water supply coverage. Given the district's unique island geography and recurring summer water scarcity, monthly DWSM meetings are being conducted to review water availability and plan long-term sustainability measures. Discussions focus on rejuvenation of existing water sources, construction of ponds, ring wells, and water treatment plants, as well as expediting Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) clearances, which often delay project implementation due to the district's extensive forest cover. To address seasonal water shortages, the district has adopted a decentralized approach by creating village-level water storage structures and enhancing local water security through convergence with MGNREGA and other development programmes. The administration is also working closely with ISRO's National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) to identify and study spring sources, assess groundwater feasibility, and improve recharge measures. The district has placed strong emphasis on water quality monitoring, with regular sample testing through WQMIS-enabled laboratories and continuous surveillance of drinking water sources. A proactive grievance redressal mechanism, supported by digital communication platforms and local stakeholder networks, helps ensure prompt resolution of complaints, including a focus on zero-leakage service delivery. Awareness campaigns on water conservation, social water audits, community training, and public outreach through print and social media are being conducted extensively to promote responsible water use and strengthen long-term source sustainability in the island district.

In his concluding remarks, Shri Kamal Kishore Soan, AS&MD, NJJM appreciated the presentations made by Districts and urged that all Mission Directors to actively participate in the upcoming Skilling and Nal Jal Mitra Programme discussions by coordinating with the State Skill Development Departments and sharing inputs before the virtual meeting scheduled on 21 September 2026. Further, he stated that States/UTs were also advised to commence geo-tagging of rural water supply sources from 2 October 2026. Further, Jal Arpan activities should be organized on 2 October 2026 across the maximum possible number of Gram Panchayats, with details of participating GPs to be shared with the Department by 20 September 2026. States/UTs were also directed to initiate post-monsoon testing of water supply sources from 2 October 2026. The meeting concluded with appreciation for the efforts of all participating States and Districts towards effective implementation of the Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0.

2310528.title: In the presence of Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah and Union Jal Shakti Minister Shri C. R. Patil, CMs of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan, Delhi and Haryana signed the Kishau Multipurpose Project agreement
2310528.body_html:
Ministry of Home Affairs
In the presence of Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah and Union Jal Shakti Minister Shri C. R. Patil, CMs of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan, Delhi and Haryana signed the Kishau Multipurpose Project agreement
This agreement is an excellent example of Modi Ji’s “Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas aur Sabka Prayas” and the core mantra of Team India
Gratitude to all the Chief Ministers for making this decades-pending project successful by following Modi Ji’s mantra of ‘Samvad se Samadhan’
Under the Modi government, this tenth water dispute is set to be resolved today
The agreement reached today will benefit all these states — Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Rajasthan and Delhi
The period from 2018 to 2026 will be known as the era of resolving water disputes in North India through mutual consensus under the leadership of Modi Ji
The Kishau Multipurpose Project agreement will prove extremely beneficial for both Delhi and the Yamuna; it will give a boost to environmental conservation
The Kishau Multipurpose Project has been declared a national project approximately 90% of its financial burden will be borne by the Government of India, and the remaining 10% by the partner states
Under the Kishau Multipurpose Project agreement, a 232.6-metre-high concrete gravity dam will be constructed on the Tons River flowing along the border of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh, with a water storage capacity of 1,562 million cubic metres
Delhi will get the biggest benefit from the Kishau Multipurpose Project agreement
Under the project, 97,000 hectares of land will be irrigated and 1,476 million units of clean hydropower will also be generated
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 5:26PM by PIB Delhi

In the presence of Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah and Union Jal Shakti Minister Shri C. R. Patil, the Chief Ministers of Uttar Pradesh Shri Yogi Adityanath, Uttarakhand Shri Pushkar Singh Dhami, Himachal Pradesh Shri Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu, Rajasthan Shri Bhajan Lal Sharma, Delhi Smt. Rekha Gupta, and Haryana Shri Nayab Singh Saini today signed the Kishau Multipurpose Project agreement. On this occasion, the Union Home Secretary, the Secretary of the Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation, and the Chief Secretaries of the concerned states were also present.

Addressing the meeting, Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that today we have witnessed a historic agreement. He expressed confidence that once the project is completed, this event will become an important chapter in history. He said that the agreement reached today will benefit Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Rajasthan and Delhi in one way or another. Shri Shah said that the most important aspect is that all six states have given their consent and signed the agreement. Union Home Minister congratulated the Chief Ministers of all six states and Union Minister for Jal Shakti Shri C. R. Patil for playing an important role in bringing the project to this stage. He said that the Government of India and the Chief Ministers of these six states of the Yamuna basin are committed to completing the project at the earliest.

Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah said that since Shri Narendra Modi became Prime Minister, this is the tenth water dispute that is now set to be resolved. He said that under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s leadership, an initiative has been undertaken to resolve serious disputes that had continued for the past fifty years. He said that first, in August 2018, the dispute over the Lakhwar Multipurpose Project was resolved. In the same month, the dispute over the Shahpur Kandi Dam Project was settled. In 2019, the dispute over the Renukaji Multipurpose Dam Project in the Upper Yamuna Basin was resolved. In 2021, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh reached an agreement on the Ken-Betwa Link Project, benefiting the water-stressed region of Bundelkhand. The revised Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal River Link project moved forward in 2024. The scheme for transferring water from Hathinikund to the Yamuna through an underground pipeline was approved in February 2024. The dispute over the rehabilitation of families displaced by the Narmada Project was resolved in July 2026. The dispute over water sharing between Bihar and Jharkhand in the Son Basin was settled in August 2026 and today, finally, an agreement has been reached on the Kishau Multipurpose Project.

Shri Amit Shah said that the period from 2018 to 2026, under the leadership of Modi Ji, will be remembered as a period in which almost all water disputes, from Kashmir to Uttar Pradesh, were resolved. He said that the foundation for these resolutions was laid in meetings of the Zonal Councils and the Ministry of Jal Shakti efficiently took these agreements forward. He said that after becoming Minister of Jal Shakti, Shri C. R. Patil took upon himself the responsibility of resolving long-pending disputes. He took initiatives at every level and, wherever assistance was required whether it was activating the Inter-State Council or involving the Ministry of Home Affairs, ensured that the task was brought to its conclusion.

Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah said that with regard to the Kishau Multipurpose Project, an agreement was reached on 12 May 1994 that separate agreements would be entered into for each storage project coming up in the basin. Without that arrangement, this would not have been possible. Subsequently, after the disputes concerning the Lakhwar and Renukaji projects were resolved in 2019, work on Kishau moved forward. Formal agreement on the project was reached on 16 June this year. The Ministry of Jal Shakti took the matter forward and after securing the consent of all the states, while considering the technical and economic aspects and safeguarding the interests of all the states, brought the matter to a resolution.

Union Home Minister said that under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, the Government of India has declared the Kishau Multipurpose Project a National Project. The Government of India will bear approximately 90 per cent of its financial burden, while the remaining 10 per cent will be borne by the participating states in accordance with the 1994 agreement. He said that the Government of Uttarakhand had certain difficulties. On behalf of the Government of India, we have assured them that efforts will be made to accommodate their demands under the schemes of the Government of India, and going forward, we will also assist Uttarakhand in bearing the financial burden that may fall upon the state.

Shri Amit Shah said that a 232.6-metre-high concrete gravity dam will be constructed on the Tons River, which flows along the border of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh, with a water storage capacity of 1,562 million cubic metres. It will irrigate 97,000 hectares of land and generate 1,476 million units of clean hydropower. He said that Delhi will be the biggest beneficiary of the project.

Union Home Minister said that when the waters of the Yamuna were allocated, there was a serious lapse on the part of policymakers. The environmental flow of the Yamuna was not calculated at all, and all the available water was distributed among the states. No water was left for the river itself. He said that 25 per cent of the water will become available through the Kishau Multipurpose Project Agreement, which will prove extremely beneficial for both Delhi and the Yamuna. It will also contribute to environmental conservation.

Shri Amit Shah said that ever since Smt. Rekha Gupta became the Chief Minister of Delhi, continuous work has been underway under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s leadership to clean the Yamuna. He expressed confidence that we will be able to achieve the goal of a clean Yamuna by 2029. When the Yamuna becomes clean, the Ganga also becomes clean, because ultimately the Yamuna merges with the Ganga at Prayagraj. He said that until the dream of cleaning the Yamuna is fulfilled, the dream of a clean Ganga will also remain incomplete.

Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah said that the Chief Minister of Delhi and all concerned stakeholders are moving forward with full cooperation and dedication towards making the Yamuna clean. He said that today’s success is an excellent example of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s guiding mantra of “Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas and Sabka Prayas” and the core mantra of Team India. It also reflects the vision of India in which everyone moves forward together. He expressed confidence that just as all the parties worked with a common purpose and in the same direction to reach this agreement, all the states will similarly work in one direction to complete the project. This will enable us to clean the Yamuna at the earliest and provide crores of people with water for drinking, agriculture, development and industrial use.

***

2310526.title: CCPA Imposed ₹10 Lakh Penalty on Rapido for Misleading Tipping Prompts and Dark Patterns
2310526.ministry: Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution
2310526.body_html:
Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution
CCPA Imposed ₹10 Lakh Penalty on Rapido for Misleading Tipping Prompts and Dark Patterns
CCPA finds “Confirm Shaming” and “Interface Interference” in Rapido’s ride-booking interface
CCPA directs Rapido to discontinue misleading prompts and practices that steer consumers towards paying more
CCPA’s action follows sector-wide examination of advance-tipping and dynamic pricing practices by ride-hailing platforms
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 5:24PM by PIB Delhi

The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), headed by Chief Commissioner Smt. Nidhi Khare and Commissioner Shri Anupam Mishra, has imposed a penalty of ₹10 lakh on Roppen Transportation Services Private Limited, which operates the ride-hailing platform Rapido, for misleading advertisements, unfair trade practices, unfair contract and dark patterns in the manner in which riders were prompted to pay more before their rides were confirmed.

The action follows a sector-wide examination of cab and bike-taxi aggregator platforms operating in India undertaken by CCPA to examine practices relating to pre-ride tipping and dynamic pricing. During its examination of various platforms, CCPA found that the Rapido app displayed prompts such as “Higher the price, higher the chance of getting a ride” and “Captains aren't accepting at ₹60. Try adding +10, +20, +30” while a rider’s booking was still being processed.

CCPA finds prompts amount to “Confirm Shaming”

CCPA found that Rapido’s algorithm first quoted a fare to the rider and, after the rider booked at that fare, prompted the rider to pay more on the ground that Captains were not accepting the original price. CCPA held that this practice creates a false impression that a rider’s chances of getting a ride quickly depend on paying an additional amount, at the precise stage when the rider has already committed to the booking and has limited scope to negotiate.The practice was held to constitute “Confirm Shaming”, a dark pattern identified under the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023, as it creates a sense of urgency and fear of losing the ride if the consumer does not agree to pay more.

Colour-coded pricing slider found to be a second dark pattern

CCPA also examined Rapido’s “Set your price” slider and found that it was colour-coded to influence the rider’s pricing decision.

  • Raising the price displayed “higher chance of getting a ride” in green.
  • Lowering the price triggered a red or orange warning.
  • The slider provided more room to increase the price than to decrease it.

CCPA held that this amounted to a second dark pattern “Interface Interference”  as the design of the interface visually steered consumers towards paying a higher amount, independent of the accompanying text.

Advance payment cannot be presented as a genuine “tip”

CCPA noted that the fare displayed to a rider at the time of booking already takes into account factors including distance, time, traffic, tolls and the amount payable to the captain.In this context, CCPA found no justification for subsequently suggesting that the rider pay an additional amount for the same ride before the ride had commenced. CCPA observed that a tip is ordinarily a voluntary payment made after a service has been rendered and should not be presented as a condition for the service to be provided.

CCPA also referred to the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025, which require that any tipping feature be made available only after completion of the ride, and not at the time of booking or during the ride. Rapido had argued that tipping is voluntary, that its matching algorithm continues to operate irrespective of whether a rider pays an additional amount, and that the prompts merely reflected real-time negotiation similar to an offline conversation between a rider and a driver.

CCPA rejected these submissions, holding that the timing and design of the prompts placed pressure on the rider at the very moment when the rider was most dependent on the platform’s further noted that Rapido had not placed any data on record demonstrating that paying an additional amount actually increases the likelihood of a rider getting a ride. The claim was therefore held to be unsubstantiated and misleading.

Sector-wide scrutiny of ride-hailing platforms

The action against Rapido forms part of CCPA’s wider scrutiny of advance-tip and dark-pattern practices across ride-hailing and bike-taxi platforms. CCPA had earlier issued notices to platforms including Uber, Ola, Rapido and Namma Yatri, directing them to comply with the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 and submit self-declarations regarding compliance. CCPA’s examination of Uber and Ola in this regard is currently ongoing.

CCPA reiterates commitment to consumer protection

In exercise of its statutory mandate under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, CCPA continues to take proactive measures to protect consumers as a class, prevent unfair trade practices and ensure that no false or misleading advertisement is made in respect of goods or services.Consumers having complaints or grievances relating to misleading advertisements, unfair trade practices or dark patterns may register their grievances through the National Consumer Helpline (NCH) at 1915 or write to CCPA at com-ccpa[at]gov[dot]in.

The Final Order is available on the CCPA website.

2310523.title: GATC Network Expands to Strengthen Legal Metrology Verification Infrastructure Across the Country
2310523.ministry: Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution
2310523.body_html:
Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution
GATC Network Expands to Strengthen Legal Metrology Verification Infrastructure Across the Country
Fresh applications from industry, laboratories and technical institutions under process
51 Government Approved Test Centres already recognised; network set to expand further
Several States notify GATC Rules in alignment with amended central framework
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 5:21PM by PIB Delhi

The Department of Consumer Affairs, Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution, is strengthening the country’s Legal Metrology verification infrastructure through the expanding network of Government Approved Test Centres (GATCs). A fresh round of applications for recognition has received strong response from industry, laboratories and technical institutions across the country.

Following amendments to the Legal Metrology (Government Approved Test Centre) Rules, 2013, the scope of GATCs has been broadened to cover 23 categories of weighing and measuring instruments across sectors including healthcare, energy, transport, retail, manufacturing, infrastructure and emerging clean-energy sectors.

The Department has continued to invite eligible industries, laboratories, engineering colleges, polytechnics, ITIs and testing facilities to seek recognition as GATCs. Applications were once again invited through the Department’s online portal, with the latest application window receiving active response from prospective applicants.

A number of applications have been received from eligible organisations following the latest call and are presently under process by the Department in consultation with the concerned State Legal Metrology Departments.

The applications are being examined for:

  • Completeness of documentation;
  • Adequacy of verification infrastructure;
  • Availability of qualified technical personnel; and
  • Site inspection prior to grant of recognition.

With 51 GATCs already recognised and a healthy pipeline of applications under active consideration, the GATC network is set to expand further in the coming months, widening the base of technically competent verification facilities available to industry and consumers.

Key Highlights

  • Fresh round of applications for GATC recognition invited, with strong response from industry, laboratories and technical institutions.
  • Applications received are under process, with site inspections and technical verification being carried out in coordination with State Legal Metrology Departments.
  • 51 GATCs have already been recognised, with the network set to expand further as more applications are approved.
  • Several States have finalised and notified their own GATC Rules, aligning them with the amended central framework.
  • Verification scope covers 23 categories of instruments, including water, gas and energy meters, breath analysers, vehicle speedometers, weighing instruments and fuel dispensers for petrol, diesel, CNG, LPG, LNG and hydrogen.
  • The expanded network strengthens Ease of Doing Business while reinforcing consumer protection, in line with India’s status as an OIML Certification Authority.

Several States align GATC Rules with amended central framework

In a significant development reinforcing the Centre-State partnership underpinning the GATC framework, several States have finalised and notified their own GATC Rules in line with the amended central framework. This alignment at the State level is expected to further deepen the reach of the verification ecosystem, enable smoother coordination between State Legal Metrology Departments and recognised GATCs, and support faster and more localised verification services for businesses and consumers across the country.

GATCs supplement State Legal Metrology infrastructure

The expansion of the GATC network is a significant step in the Department’s ongoing efforts to modernise India’s Legal Metrology ecosystem. By enabling technically competent private institutions to undertake verification and re-verification of specified weights and measures, the initiative supplements the capacity of State Legal Metrology Departments.

This allows Legal Metrology Officers to devote greater attention to:

  • Market surveillance;
  • Risk-based inspections;
  • Enforcement against serious violations; and
  • Consumer grievance redressal.

Verification covers 23 categories of instruments

The expanded GATC framework covers 23 categories of weighing and measuring instruments, including:

  • Water, gas and energy meters;
  • Breath analysers;
  • Speedometers used to measure the speed of vehicles;
  • Weighing instruments; and
  • Fuel dispensers for petrol, diesel, CNG, LPG, LNG and hydrogen.

As the network of GATCs continues to grow, supported by fresh applications and the alignment of State-level rules with the central framework, the Department is steadily building a larger, more accessible and technologically capable verification infrastructure. The expansion reflects the combined efforts of the Legal Metrology system to advance Ease of Doing Business while simultaneously strengthening consumer protection and confidence in everyday commercial transactions.

The Department reiterates its commitment to building a transparent, technology-driven and self-reliant system of measurement verification that enhances fairness in trade and protects the interests of consumers across the country.

2310476.title: INDIA-US JOINT MILITARY EXERCISE YUDH ABHYAS 2026 COMMENCES AT AULI AND MAHAJAN
2310476.body_html:
Ministry of Defence
INDIA-US JOINT MILITARY EXERCISE YUDH ABHYAS 2026 COMMENCES AT AULI AND MAHAJAN
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 4:45PM by PIB Delhi

The opening ceremony of 22nd edition of India-US Joint Military Exercise Yudh Abhyas was held today at Auli Foreign Training Node in Uttarakhand. Major General Amaresh Gunjan, General Officer Commanding, 14 Infantry Division and Colonel Benjamin Jackman, Commander, 1st Infantry Brigade Combat Team, 11th Airborne Division, US Army, addressed the participating contingents comprising of 600 personnel from each side. The exercise is simultaneously being conducted at Auli and Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan.

The exercise is aimed at enhancing the joint military capability of both armies for employment of Integrated Battle Groups in mountainous and semi-mountainous terrain, with emphasis on infantry-dominated operations. It will strengthen interoperability, facilitate exchanges of best operational practices and strengthen joint planning and execution.

Technology infusion will form a key focus area. The training will include the employment of drones and autonomous systems for surveillance and reconnaissance as well as demonstration of contemporary weapon systems will be undertaken at Mahajan Field Firing Ranges. Subject Matter Experts from both Armies will also exchange views on emerging technologies and developments in multi-domain warfare.

The exercise provides an opportunity for both Armies to share tactics, techniques and procedures; and enhance their ability to undertake coordinated military operations across varied terrain and operational environment.

2310460.title: Union Minister Dr Jitendra Singh Inaugurates Indigenous SPROUT Facility at BRIC-NIPGR to Accelerate Development of Climate-Resilient Crops
2310460.body_html:
Ministry of Science & Technology
Union Minister Dr Jitendra Singh Inaugurates Indigenous SPROUT Facility at BRIC-NIPGR to Accelerate Development of Climate-Resilient Crops
SPROUT will enable crop research under different environmental conditions, helping connect genomics and gene technologies with faster trait evaluation and crop improvement says Dr Jitendra Singh
India witnessing simultaneous advances in plant and human biotechnology as part of BioE3 policy and the biotechnology push of Modi Government: Dr Jitendra Singh
SpeedSeed technology can reduce chickpea generation cycle to around 40 days, considerably shortening breeding timelines: Dr. Jitendra Singh
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 4:31PM by PIB Delhi

Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences and MoS PMO, Dr. Jitendra Singh today inaugurated the "SpeedSeed Phenotyping and Resource Optimization for Unified Trait Analysis" (SPROUT) facility at BRIC-National Institute of Plant Genome Research (BRIC-NIPGR), New Delhi, describing it as an important indigenous capability for developing climate-resilient crops suited to different weather conditions.

The Minister said that in a country as geographically and agro-climatically diverse as India, the ability to study and evaluate crops under different environmental conditions is critical for strengthening agricultural resilience. The Minister said the initiative is part of the wider BioE3 policy and the biotechnology push of the Modi Government, under which simultaneous breakthroughs are taking place in plant biotechnology as well as human biotechnology. The BioE3 policy itself includes climate-resilient agriculture among its strategic thematic sectors.

The event was attended by Prof. Manoj Prasad, Director, BRIC-NIPGR; Dr. Senthil K. Muthappa, BRIC-NIPGR; and Dr. Nitin Jain, Scientist-H, Department of Biotechnology (DBT). During the programme, Dr. Jitendra Singh inaugurated the SPROUT facility and planted a sapling under the “Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam” campaign. He also interacted with scientists and officials of BRIC-NIPGR.

SPROUT is a season-independent, controlled-environment facility designed for high-throughput phenotyping, precision stress screening and evaluation of germplasm, breeding populations, mutants, transgenic and genome-edited lines. With a major focus on chickpea, the facility will help connect advances in genomics and genome editing with precise trait evaluation and breeding. This will strengthen the ability to move more efficiently from gene discovery to trait validation and ultimately to crop improvement.

The facility comes at a time when climate change and changing weather patterns are creating an urgent need for faster agricultural solutions. Research supported in agriculture biotechnology has resulted in improved plant varieties and genotypes across economically important crops including rice, wheat, oilseeds, pulses, millets, fruits and vegetables, while work on plant microbiome interactions is opening possibilities for beneficial microorganisms to support sustainable crop productivity, soil health and nutrient availability.

Dr. Jitendra Singh said that modern biotechnology must increasingly be translated into technologies that can respond to real agricultural challenges and provide tangible benefits to farmers. He said that the scientific advances being made today, particularly in genomics, gene technologies, precision phenotyping and accelerated breeding, will become increasingly relevant in the years ahead.

NIPGR has also developed SpeedSeed, a separate technology for accelerated generation advancement. In chickpea, optimised protocols can reduce the generation cycle to approximately 40 days, considerably shortening conventional breeding and research timelines. The technology can be used within SPROUT or adapted to other suitable controlled-environment facilities. Together, SPROUT and SpeedSeed can accelerate the evaluation and advancement of promising crop traits and shorten the path from research to improved varieties.

Over the last twelve years, the Department of Biotechnology has played a transformative role in strengthening India’s agriculture biotechnology ecosystem, supporting innovation from laboratory research to farmers’ fields. Between 2014 and 2026, more than 300 projects were supported in agriculture biotechnology and allied areas. More than 50 improved varieties across rice, wheat, chickpea, mustard, vegetables and forestry species have been developed with enhanced tolerance to drought, floods, salinity, pests and diseases.

A major achievement has been the development of 17 climate-resilient rice varieties under a flagship genomics-assisted breeding programme. These varieties are now cultivated across nearly 15 lakh hectares, demonstrating the potential of advanced genomics and molecular breeding to translate scientific research into solutions with direct relevance to farmers and food security.

The Minister said that the biotechnology ecosystem is expanding beyond individual technologies and laboratories, with advances in plant biotechnology, human biotechnology, genomics and other emerging areas taking place simultaneously. He said that the country’s biotechnology journey is increasingly being driven by the convergence of advanced science, technology and applications that can address challenges relating to agriculture, health, sustainability and national development.

He also referred to the wider role of biotechnology in areas such as genetic technologies and recycling/circular approaches, stressing the need to align institutional capabilities and human-resource systems with the rapidly changing scientific landscape. The BioE3 framework similarly seeks to promote a sustainable and circular bioeconomy through convergence between biotechnology, engineering and digitalisation.

Dr. Jitendra Singh said that scientific achievements should not remain confined to laboratories or scientific institutions and called for a stronger culture of science communication and public outreach. He said that official visits to scientific institutions should not be limited to formal engagement or publicity, but should help those for whom the technologies are being developed understand what is being done and how it benefits them.

He suggested greater use of short films, workshops and professionally produced visual content to explain scientific technologies in an accessible manner. Such communication, he said, could show the challenges that existed before a technology was developed, explain how the scientific intervention addressed those challenges and demonstrate the relief or benefit that the technology has brought to farmers, industry and other users. Technical experts and professional communicators could work together to present these stories in a manner that has greater public and media impact.

The Minister also called for stronger interaction between scientific institutions and industry partners, farmers and other stakeholders. He said that regular institutional meetings and presentations should provide opportunities for people from outside the immediate scientific ecosystem to participate, so that scientists and stakeholders can understand each other’s work and identify opportunities for collaboration.

Referring to the experience of CSIR institutions, Dr. Jitendra Singh said that regular meetings can be used as platforms for scientific presentations and for bringing external stakeholders into discussions. He encouraged BRIC-NIPGR and other institutions to adopt similar practices and involve industry partners and other relevant stakeholders in institutional interactions so that the benefits of scientific research can reach beyond the scientific community.

He also stressed the importance of taking farmers into scientific institutions and allowing them to see the work being carried out there. Recalling his experience with CSIR institutions, the Minister said that farmers who had never previously visited such research establishments could develop misconceptions about the nature of the work being undertaken. Direct interaction and exposure, he said, can remove such apprehensions and help farmers understand how modern science and biotechnology are being developed for their benefit.

Dr. Jitendra Singh also referred to ongoing biotechnology initiatives involving experimental kits and scientific work in this emerging space, including the use of kits from a biotechnology laboratory in Delhi for experiments, and said that such developments should also find appropriate space in the wider communication of India’s biotechnology progress.

He said that institutions must continuously adapt their communication and human-resource practices to current scientific and technological trends, rather than relying only on conventional approaches. Scientific organisations, he added, need to become more vocal and visible in communicating their achievements so that society, industry and potential beneficiaries are aware of the work being undertaken.

The Minister said that the technologies being developed in biotechnology today are futuristic in nature and will become increasingly relevant in the years to come. He called for sustained efforts to communicate these advances in a manner that demonstrates what Indian science is doing for farmers, industry and society.

Facilities such as SPROUT, he said, demonstrate how modern biotechnology can contribute to the development of climate-resilient and productive crops, strengthen India’s agricultural capabilities and support the goal of a more self-reliant agriculture sector. He congratulated the scientists and technical teams of BRIC-NIPGR for developing the facility and said that such capabilities will contribute to India’s journey towards Viksit Bharat 2047.

2310452.title: From Waste Picker to Swachhta Udyami: Balamala Malli's Journey Towards Dignity and Self-Reliance
2310452.body_html:
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment
From Waste Picker to Swachhta Udyami: Balamala Malli's Journey Towards Dignity and Self-Reliance
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 4:20PM by PIB Delhi

The limited income, social exclusion and lack of educational opportunities can restrict the possibility of building a secure future for sanitation workers from economically disadvantaged communities. Timely financial assistance and access to mechanised sanitation equipment can help transform such vulnerable livelihoods into safer and more sustainable sources of income.

Demonstrating the impact of support under the Swachhta Udyami Yojana (SUY) component of the NAMASTE Scheme, Shri Balamala Malli, a 30-year-old member of the Scheduled Tribe community, has moved towards greater economic stability and dignity. As part of a five-member group project, he received assistance to procure a 3-in-1 Jetting, Grabbing and Rodding Machine, which created an additional livelihood opportunity for him and the other group members.

Shri Malli has worked as a waste picker with the Guntur Municipal Corporation in Andhra Pradesh, for the past ten years. He worked six days a week and earned approximately Rs. 150 to Rs. 200 per day.

Poverty had prevented Mr. Malli from attending school. His parents were extremely poor, and he began accompanying them in waste-picking activities at a young age instead of receiving a formal education. As an illiterate member of the Scheduled Tribe community living in an urban slum, he also faced social discrimination, exclusion and limited access to essential amenities and services.

His wife is a homemaker, and the couple have three children studying in elementary school. Despite the family's difficult socioeconomic circumstances, Mr. Malli aspired to become economically self-sufficient and provide his children with quality education and a better future.

On 19 June 2023, financial assistance was provided by the National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation (NSKFDC) under SUY for a group project comprising Shri Malli and four other members. The support enabled the group to procure a 3-in-1 Jetting, Grabbing and Rodding Machine for mechanised sanitation work.

The project had a total cost of Rs. 49,40,710. It was supported through a loan amount of Rs. 30,80,530 and an upfront capital subsidy of Rs. 18,60,180. Access to the machine enhanced the group's livelihood opportunities and enabled its members to undertake sanitation operations through safer and more efficient mechanical methods.

Before receiving assistance, Shri Malli earned approximately Rs. 8,000 per month through waste-picking activities. Following the procurement of the 3-in-1 machine, he began earning an additional Rs. 10,000 per month, increasing his total monthly income to approximately Rs. 18,000.

The increase in income has enabled Shri Malli to meet household expenses more comfortably, support his children's education and address several of the economic challenges that previously affected his family. The intervention has strengthened his livelihood and helped him lead a more stable and dignified life.

Shri Malli's journey shows how financial assistance, collective enterprise and mechanised sanitation equipment can improve livelihood security for sanitation workers. From relying on low-paid waste-picking work, he has become part of a group enterprise with improved earning opportunities and greater confidence about his family's future.

Talking about the support, Shri Malli said, “The support helped me increase my income and provide better education and a more secure future for my children. I now feel more confident about supporting my family and living with dignity.”

Today, he is working towards economic self-reliance and ensuring that his children receive the education and opportunities that poverty denied him. His progress reflects the role of the SUY component of the NAMASTE Scheme in advancing safety, dignity and sustainable livelihoods among sanitation workers.

2310427.title: Press Note on Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) Monthly Bulletin August 2026
2310427.body_html:
Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation
Press Note on Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) Monthly Bulletin August 2026
Overall LFPR increased further
WPR strengthened in rural areas and stable in urban areas
Rural UR recorded decline
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 4:00PM by PIB Delhi

Snapshot:

  • The overall LFPR (15+ years) increased to 55.6% in August, 2026, up from 55.4% in July, 2026.
  • LFPR (15+ years and above) in rural areas stood at 58.2% in August, 2026, registering an increase of 1.2 percentage points over August 2025.
  • Overall female LFPR (15+ years and above) recorded at 34.8% in August, 2026, 1.1 percentage points higher than the level recorded in August, 2025.
  • Overall WPR (15+ years and above) increased to 52.8% in August 2026,the highest level recorded since March, 2026.
  • Rural WPR (15+ years and above) increased by 1.3 percentage points year-on-year to 55.8% in August, 2026.
  • Overall UR (15+ years and above) remained stable at 5.0% in August, 2026.
  • Rural UR declined to 4.1% in August, 2026, the lowest level recorded since January 2026.

A. Introduction

The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) conducted by NSO, MoSPI, is the primary source of data on activity participation and employment and unemployment conditions of the population. The PLFS survey methodology has been modified from January, 2025 to provide monthly and quarterly estimates of labour force indicators for the country.

Monthly results of PLFS are released in the form of Monthly Bulletins. It presents estimates of key labour market indicators viz. Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR), Worker Population Ratio (WPR) and Unemployment Rate (UR) at the all-India level following the Current Weekly Status[1] (CWS) approach.

The Monthly Bulletins for April, 2025 to July, 2026 have already been released. The present Monthly Bulletin for August, 2026 is the seventeenth in the series.

Key findings for persons of age 15 years and above following CWS:

  • Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) strengthened:

The overall Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) for persons aged 15 years and above increased to 55.6% in August, 2026, from 55.4% in July, 2026. A similar trend has also been observed in rural areas, where the LFPR for persons aged 15 years and above increased to 58.2% in August, 2026, from 58.0% in July, 2026. In urban areas, LFPR remained constant at 50.4% in August, 2026 as compared to the previous month.

Compared to the corresponding month of the previous year, the overall LFPR increased by 0.6 percentage point, from 55.0% in August, 2025 to 55.6% in August, 2026. During the same period, rural LFPR also increased by 1.2 percentage points, from 57.0% to 58.2%, while urban LFPR experienced a marginal decline of 0.5 percentage point, from 50.9% to 50.4%.    

 

Rural LFPR registered an increase of 1.2 percentage points over the corresponding month of the previous year, reaching 58.2% in August, 2026

 

  • Female Labour Force Participation exhibits upward momentum:

The overall female LFPR experienced a moderate increase from 34.4% in July, 2026 to 34.8% in August, 2026 mainly contributed by rural female LFPR which increased to 39.4% during the current month from 38.8% recorded in the previous month. During the same period, female LFPR in urban areas was broadly stable at 25.4% compared to 25.3% observed in July, 2026.

Over the year, the overall female LFPR increased by 1.1 percentage points, from 33.7% in August, 2025 to 34.8% in August, 2026. During the same period, female LFPR in rural areas increased by 2.0 percentage points, from 37.4% to 39.4%, while urban female LFPR declined by 0.7 percentage point, from 26.1% to 25.4%.

Overall female LFPR increased for the second consecutive month, reaching 34.8% in August 2026
  • Rise in rural workforce participation across genders:

The overall WPR increased from 52.5% in July, 2026 to 52.8% in August, 2026 driven by increased workforce participation in rural areas. WPR in rural areas recorded an increase to 55.8% in August, 2026 from 55.4% in the previous month while urban WPR maintained the same level of 47.0% in August, 2026 as observed in July, 2026.  

The overall WPR showing an increase of 0.6 percentage point over the corresponding month of the previous year from 52.2% in August, 2025 to 52.8% in August, 2026. During the same period, rural WPR increased by 1.3 percentage points from 54.5% to 55.8%, whereas the urban WPR stood at 47.0% in August, 2026 from 47.5% in August, 2025, experienced a decline of 0.5 percentage point.



 

Year-on-year comparison indicates an increase in the overall female WPR, rising to 33.0% in August, 2026 from 32.0% recorded in August, 2025.

 

  • Rural Unemployment Rate (UR) declined:

Overall UR among persons of age 15 years and above declined marginally from 5.1% in July, 2026 to 5.0% in August, 2026. During the same period, rural UR decreased from 4.5% to 4.1%, while urban UR remained almost stable at 6.8% in August, 2026 compared to 6.7% in July, 2026.

Compared with August, 2025, the overall UR and urban UR remained broadly stable in August, 2026, whereas the rural UR declined by 0.2 percentage point from 4.3% in August, 2025 to 4.1% in August, 2026.

 

Since January, 2026, rural UR recorded its lowest level of 4.1% in August, 2026

 

  • Rural UR decreased across gender:

The overall UR among male aged 15 years and above declined for the three consecutive months, reaching 4.9% in August, 2026 from 5.4% in May, 2026. The rural male UR declined from 4.6% in July, 2026 to 4.3% in August, 2026, while urban male UR marginally up from 5.9% to 6.1% during the same period. Among female of age 15 years and above, overall UR declined in two consecutive months to 5.1% in August, 2026 from 5.9% in June, 2026. Rural female UR decreased from 4.3% in July, 2026 to 3.9% in August, 2026 while urban female UR remained broadly stable compared to previous month.

A year-on-year comparison indicates that the overall UR for both male and female remained broadly unchanged in August, 2026. 

 

The overall male and female UR declined in August, 2026 compared to July, 2026

 

At the all-India level, the monthly estimates are based on information collected from a total number of 3,70,160 persons surveyed.

2310434.title: From Financial Barriers to Doctoral Achievement: Shewani Kumari's Journey towards Academic Excellence
2310434.body_html:
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment
From Financial Barriers to Doctoral Achievement: Shewani Kumari's Journey towards Academic Excellence
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 3:41PM by PIB Delhi

Financial help and support can make higher education and advanced research feasible and possible for students from socially and economically disadvantaged backgrounds. Fellowship assistance can provide the stability required to meet academic expenses, continue research and work towards long-term professional goals.

Shewani Kumari, a 29-year-old scholar from the Scheduled Caste community, overcame financial, social and educational barriers to complete her Ph.D. in Sociology. She is presently working as a lecturer and aspires to become an Assistant Professor.

Coming from a family with limited income, Shewani faced considerable difficulty in meeting the costs of higher education and research. Expenses related to tuition, books, research materials, travel and other academic activities placed a significant burden on the family and created uncertainty about the continuation of her studies.

Limited access to academic resources, professional guidance and quality educational opportunities added to these challenges. Social and geographical limitations also restricted her exposure to advanced academic and career opportunities.

Despite these barriers, Shewani remained committed to her education. She viewed academic achievement as a means of building a better future for her family and improving its socio-economic condition through professional success.

Financial assistance through the NFSDC Fellowship for Higher Education and Research became an important source of support in her academic journey. She received Rs. 31,000 per month as a Junior Research Fellow and Rs. 35,000 per month as a Senior Research Fellow.

The fellowship helped her meet essential educational and research expenses and enabled her to continue her work with greater financial stability. It also provided encouragement and strengthened her confidence to pursue her academic goals.

With the support of the fellowship and her sustained determination, Shewani successfully completed her Ph.D. in Sociology and gained teaching experience. These achievements have strengthened her academic and professional position.

At present, Shewani is working as a lecturer and progressing towards her aspiration of becoming an Assistant Professor. Her journey demonstrates how timely financial assistance can enable scholars from disadvantaged communities to overcome structural barriers and pursue advanced education.

Expressing her wish to move ahead for next level in professional career, Shewani Kumari said, “The fellowship gave me the financial support and confidence to continue my research and complete my Ph.D. Today, as a lecturer, I am closer to fulfilling my dream of becoming an Assistant Professor and creating a better future through education."

Shewani's success reflects the transformative role of fellowship support in expanding access to research and professional opportunities. Her achievement is an example of perseverance strengthened by institutional assistance and educational opportunity.

2310405.title: From Addiction and Distress to Recovery and Stability: Dev M's Journey through Counselling and Rehabilitation
2310405.body_html:
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment
From Addiction and Distress to Recovery and Stability: Dev M's Journey through Counselling and Rehabilitation
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 2:58PM by PIB Delhi

Addiction can affect not only an individual's health but also family relationships, livelihood, emotional well-being and social standing. Timely counselling, medical treatment and sustained follow-up can help a person understand addiction-related triggers, develop healthier coping mechanisms and move steadily towards recovery and rehabilitation.

Demonstrating the value of coordinated rehabilitation support, Dev M (name changed), a 29-year-old self-employed man from the OBC community in Akola district, Maharashtra, received counselling and medical treatment through the Purogami Bhaiyyuprasad Samaj Kalyan Vikas Vyayam Prasark Sanstha, an Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts (IRCA). The intervention helped strengthen his recovery process and contributed positively to his overall well-being.

Before receiving support, Dev was facing multiple family, financial and social challenges that had significantly affected his personal and professional life. Addiction contributed to financial difficulties, and its adverse impact was also reflected in the performance of his business and his overall economic stability.

Frequent family conflicts and strained relationships created an emotionally stressful environment for Dev and those around him. At the same time, social stigma and disrespectful treatment affected his mental well-being and weakened his confidence. These combined pressures made it more difficult for him to regain stability in his personal life and livelihood.

Despite these challenges, Dev aspired to overcome addiction completely, improve his family relationships and lead a peaceful and stable life. He also wanted to develop better emotional control and seek support from trusted individuals whenever he faced stress or difficulties.

On 5 October 2025, Dev received support through the IRCA in Akola. As part of the rehabilitation process, he was provided free medical treatment, psychological therapy, family counselling, addiction-related medicines, free food during treatment and regular follow-up services.

Through individual, group and family counselling sessions, Dev received guidance to address his personal challenges and recognise the triggers associated with addiction. The sessions also helped him understand how stress, strained relationships and emotional difficulties could influence his behaviour and recovery.

Dev was introduced to practical stress-management techniques, including deep-breathing exercises, maintaining a daily activity diary and engaging in regular physical exercise. He was also encouraged to discuss his concerns with trusted individuals instead of facing difficult situations alone. These measures supported the development of healthier responses to stress and addiction-related triggers.

Counselling and medical treatment provided the structured support required to facilitate his recovery and rehabilitation. Family counselling helped address strained relationships, while regular follow-up reinforced the guidance received during treatment and strengthened his commitment to the recovery process.

The intervention has contributed positively to Dev's overall well-being and helped him move towards better emotional control, improved family relations and a more stable life. Continued counselling, medical care and follow-up support have remained important components of his rehabilitation journey.

Talking about the facilitation, Dev M expressed his views, “Counselling and medical care helped me gain better emotional control, improve my family relationships and move towards a more stable life.”

Dev's experience highlights how accessible treatment, psychological support, family participation and regular follow-up can help individuals facing addiction work towards recovery with dignity. His journey reflects the importance of timely institutional support in enabling beneficiaries to rebuild confidence, restore relationships and move towards a peaceful and productive future.

2310404.title: Astronomy enthusiasts from across India participate in the fourth HDSR Star Party
2310404.body_html:
Ministry of Science & Technology
Astronomy enthusiasts from across India participate in the fourth HDSR Star Party
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 2:56PM by PIB Delhi

Expert astrophotographers and amateur astronomers from across the country participated in the fourth edition of the Hanle Dark Sky Reserve Star Party from 7 – 12 September, 2026 at the Indian Astronomical Observatory in Hanle, Ladakh.

“The enthusiasm with which amateur astronomers as well as astrophotographers from across the country participated, highlighted the event’s role in underlining the importance of preserving its pristine dark skies, both for scientific research and for the public, said Prof. Annapurni Subramaniam, Director of IIA.

Around 40 amateur astronomers from Chandigarh, Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, New Delhi, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh. These selected participants travelled to Leh with their advanced equipment, to fully utilise the four nights under the dark skies of Hanle at the event organised jointly by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Department of Wildlife Protection of UT Ladakh, Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR).

The Open Night for the local communities and the nearby tourists on 10th September saw footfalls of more than 1200 people. 

The Star Party participants, along with the HDSR Astronomy Ambassadors and the Observatory staff showed the visitors through specially designated amateur telescopes and answered their myriad questions throughout the evening. Senior officials from various organisations in the area were also invited to look through telescopes and were briefed on the importance of curtailing light pollution in the region.

Special training sessions were organised every evening for the HDSR Astronomy Ambassadors, the 25 local villagers who have been trained to conduct astronomy tours for tourists for the past three years, and who have been supplied with telescopes by the government of Ladakh. The expert participants also acted as mentors and helped in teaching many practical aspects of night sky watching and astrophotography to the Ambassadors.

The Hanle Dark Sky Reserve (HDSR) in Ladakh is renowned for its exceptionally dark night sky, making it a highly attractive location for astrophotographers and amateur astronomers. Notified as a dark sky reserve by the Government of Ladakh in December 2022, HDSR represents a novel astronomy based socio-economic development initiative. It is built on two key concepts: reducing light pollution for the benefit of continued research at the Observatory, and promoting astro-tourism that creates benefits for local communities.

The success of HDSR is enabled by the strong commitment of various stakeholders, including the UT Ladakh administration. HDSR is anchored by the Indian Astronomical Observatory at Hanle. The Observatory is operated by the IIA, an autonomous institution under the Department of Science and Technology (DST).

The annual HDSR Star Party underscores the importance of preserving the dark skies of Hanle for the future, and the diverse set of stakeholders for whom the Hanle skies are a vital and rare resource. “With the 3.7-m upgraded Himalayan Chandra Telescope and the 13.7-m National Large Optical-infrared Telescope that are proposed to come up in Hanle, it is imperative that we come together to safeguard its dark skies”, said Prof DK Sahu of IIA, Scientist in charge of the Observatory.

Fig: Group photo of the HDSR Star Party 2026 participants (credit: Ajay Talwar)

2310401.title: Vice-President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan addresses 25th Anniversary Celebrations of ICWA as an Institute of National Importance
2310401.body_html:
Vice President's Secretariat
Vice-President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan addresses 25th Anniversary Celebrations of ICWA as an Institute of National Importance
Vice-President Congratulates EAM Dr. S. Jaishankar and the MEA Team on Successful BRICS Summit
Human Progress and World Peace Possible Only When Nations Recognise Each Other’s Concerns and Work for Mutual Benefit: Vice-President
“India Is Emerging on Global Stage as a Strong Voice for Peace, Progress & Prosperity”: Vice-President 
Posted On: 15 SEP 2026 2:34PM by PIB Delhi

Vice-President and President, Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA), Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan today addressed the 25th Anniversary celebrations of ICWA as an Institution of National Importance at Sapru House, New Delhi. He said the Silver Jubilee was an occasion for gratitude and reflection and paid tribute to the founders, former leaders, Directors General, scholars, diplomats, researchers and staff who have contributed to the Council’s distinguished legacy.

Vice President of India and President, Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA), Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan addressed the 25th Anniversary celebrations of ICWA as an Institution of National Importance at Sapru House, New Delhi today.

The Vice President emphasised that human… pic.twitter.com/gFWfDUaqTy

— Vice-President of India (@VPIndia) September 15, 2026
The Vice-President congratulated External Affairs Minister and Vice-President of ICWA, Dr. S. Jaishankar, Foreign Secretary Shri Vikram Misri and the entire team of the Ministry of External Affairs for the successful hosting of the BRICS Summit. He said that in a world disturbed by conflicts and contradictions, the unanimous adoption of the New Delhi Leaders’ Declaration was a significant achievement.

He emphasised that the first objective of diplomacy is to build good relations among nations. Human progress and world peace must go hand in hand, and this is possible only when countries recognise each other’s concerns and work towards mutual benefit, he said.

Highlighting India’s growing global role under Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, the Vice-President said India has emerged as a strong voice for peace, progress and prosperity. He highlighted Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, the world is one family, and cited Vaccine Maitri during Covid crisis, India’s disaster-response efforts, LiFE and global initiatives such as the International Solar Alliance and Global Biofuel Alliance as examples of this philosophy in action.

The Vice-President highlighted India’s achievements in UPI and Digital Public Infrastructure, observing that “transparent payment systems lead to transparent governance.” He said India is sharing its technological and institutional capabilities with the Global South through ITEC and educational collaborations, including the first IIT campus outside India in Zanzibar. “India is emerging on the global stage to lead the Global South,” he said, noting the growing trust and confidence of India’s international partners.

Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan said the changing global environment has made ICWA’s role even more important. He outlined four priorities for the Council: strengthening research on India’s Neighbourhood First, Act East, Global South and Indo-Pacific priorities; expanding work on cyber security, space, critical technologies and global supply chains; deepening engagement with universities and young scholars; and becoming a reliable repository of knowledge on world affairs with an authentic Indian perspective.

The Vice-President said ICWA must prepare itself intellectually and institutionally for Viksit Bharat @ 2047 and work towards becoming one of the world’s respected centres for the study of international affairs. He expressed confidence that the Council would make even greater contributions to India and a peaceful world order by its Golden Jubilee.

The Vice-President also visited a photo exhibition showcasing ICWA’s journey and evolution and presented mementos to former Directors General in recognition of their contributions to the Council.
